title: The Resurrection Braid — grounded cross-source gaps + two-chair glosses
qud: How is the resurrection attested, and what does each account's telling withhold?
provenance: engine_braid_cross_source_scan.py (Claude Max SDK, Tier-1) over the 4 gospels coded source_move rows; two-chair select+gloss via engine_braid_chair_gloss_select_s157.py

featured_primary.beat_text: the women/witness(es) enter or peer into the tomb
featured_primary.gap: John alone records a witness (the beloved disciple) reaching belief inside the tomb through unnamed, absolute interior seeing — without any angelic speech or explicitly identified object; Mark and Luke route all interior witness-response through a named heavenly figure's address.
featured_primary.gloss: Eckhart would have recognized what John did there. The beloved disciple sees — object unnamed — and believes — content unnamed. In Eckhart's lexicon, that absence of naming isn't a gap the author forgot to fill; it's abgeschiedenheit (detachment) as epistemic form: the soul stripped of all images, receiving what it receives without mediation. Mark and Luke need the angelic voice: the evidence alone cannot produce understanding; a figure must speak before faith is possible. But for Eckhart, that speech is the medium (the intervening image or concept) that the highest knowing has to pass through and leave behind. John's disciple skips it. He enters, he sees, he believes — and the silence where object and content should be is not withholding but arrival. The empty tomb, in this reading, is not evidence toward a conclusion. It is the Grund (the groundless ground) where seeing and the thing believed have collapsed into one.
featured_primary.one_line: Object-free seeing as arrival, not absence
featured_primary.seed_note: Rests on Eckhart's Sermon 52 ('Beati pauperes spiritu') on poverty of spirit as knowing-nothing and having-nothing; his recurring ân mittel (without medium) formulation across the German sermons; 'Von Abgeschiedenheit' on detachment as the soul's highest receptive capacity; and the Grund theology throughout the Predigten — drawn from memory, not fetched text.

featured_primary.beat_text: the body of Jesus is discovered absent from its burial place
featured_primary.gap: No account records any witness deliberating over natural explanations for the body's absence — reburial, theft, mistaken tomb — before the resurrection claim is either announced or inferred; the move from 'body absent' to 'risen' skips the elimination of competing causes in every account.
featured_primary.gloss: Maimonides would name the structural failure directly. His standard — drawn from the Mishneh Torah's laws of eidut (testimony) and the epistemological commitments of the Guide — requires a specific sequence: rational grounds first, elimination of natural alternatives, then the miraculous sign. Here the sequence is inverted. The sign appears (the empty tomb), the natural alternatives are never examined, and the supernatural interpretation is advanced as self-evident. John alone raises the theft-hypothesis, but only to move past it, never to refute it by method. Every account converts 'body absent' to 'risen' without the argumentative middle. For Maimonides, this is the critical tell: the witnesses arrive already oriented toward a particular interpretation. That is not testimony — it is prior commitment finding a confirming occasion. His question of the text would be harder than any the accounts raise: what would this evidence look like to someone who did not already believe the one whose tomb they entered?
featured_primary.one_line: Sign without elimination of alternatives is not testimony
featured_primary.seed_note: Rests on Guide of the Perplexed II:25 on miracles and their relation to rational demonstration; Hilkhot Yesodei haTorah 8:1-3 on the limits of a miraculous sign's evidential force; and Hilkhot Edut on testimony standards requiring disinterested witnesses and cross-examination — drawn from memory, not fetched text.

featured_primary.beat_text: the witnesses react with fear, dread, or bewilderment
featured_primary.gap: Mark alone stages the witnesses' fear as a force that actively prevents transmission of the resurrection attestation — the women say nothing to anyone (M31) and the primary narrative closes on ongoing, cause-unnamed fear (M32); all other accounts have the witnesses overcome their fear and transmit.
featured_primary.gloss: Luther would read Mark's ending as the gospel in its most theologically honest form. His theologia crucis (theology of the cross) insists that God is found precisely where God appears absent — that resurrection power arrives sub contrariis, under its opposite. The women's paralysis isn't a narrative failure; it is the correct response to an encounter that exceeds every receiving category. The cause-unnamed fear — Mark refuses to disclose what they fear — is not an editorial gap. It is the name for anfechtung (the spiritual assault that precedes faith): the creature undone before it can speak. Matthew, Luke, and John give us the resurrection clothed in transmission: the gospel marches out, orderly, commissioned. For Luther, that is the theologia gloriae (theology of glory) reading — triumph wearing its own face. Mark gives us what the other three suppress: the word arriving into silence, paralysis, a fear that cannot yet be spoken. That silence is not the resurrection's failure. It is its first address.
featured_primary.one_line: Mark's silenced women are the theology of the cross
featured_primary.seed_note: Rests on the Heidelberg Disputation (1518), theses 19-21, on theologia crucis versus theologia gloriae and God revealed sub contrariis; De Servo Arbitrio (1525) on the Deus absconditus; and the concept of Anfechtung as elaborated throughout Luther's Psalm commentaries and early reform writings — drawn from memory, not fetched text.

featured_primary.beat_text: his absence from the tomb is explicitly declared ('he is not here')
featured_primary.gap: No account states when or how the departure from the tomb occurred — the declared absence implies a prior event (the body ceased to be here) that is universally withheld from the declaration itself and from everything surrounding it.
featured_primary.gloss: Gregory of Nyssa would not call this a gap the evangelists failed to fill. In his reading of Exodus 33, Moses asks to see God's face and is placed in a cleft of the rock as God passes — he sees only the back, only the aftermath of the passing. Gregory names this the paradigm of all divine encounter: gnophos (the luminous darkness) into which the soul advances, always arriving where God was, never where God is in the act of being. The departure from the tomb is that same structure. The witnesses reach the place; the event of leaving has already occurred and will not be re-entered. Every account points outward — to Galilee, to remembered prophecy — because that is the correct motion after such an encounter: epektasis (perpetual straining forward), the soul redirected rather than satisfied. The silence at the departure-moment is not withholding. It is the form divine transit takes when passing through what creaturely time cannot hold.
featured_primary.one_line: The empty tomb as the back of God
featured_primary.seed_note: Rests on Gregory's De Vita Moysis Part II on Moses entering the gnophos and seeing only God's back — divine presence known only in aftermath; and In Canticum Canticorum for epektasis as the soul's perpetual advance into inexhaustible divine reality. The phrase 'luminous darkness' is more precisely Pseudo-Dionysius but is continuous with Gregory's apophatic development — drawn from memory, not fetched text.

featured_primary.beat_text: his resurrected/raised status is announced (typically as divine passive)
featured_primary.gap: All three accounts withhold the agent of the raising — no account names who raised Jesus.
featured_primary.gloss: Barth would read the unnamed agent as the most theologically precise feature of these sentences, not a gap. His understanding of divine action turns on this: God is always Subject (never predicate, never object), and the resurrection is the act in which God most completely refuses to be named as an agent among agents. A grammatical subject in 'X raised Jesus' places X inside the story, locatable, controllable by the categories the sentence uses. The passivum divinum (divine passive — the grammatical form that withholds the acting God from the subject position) withdraws the raiser from that slot not from ignorance but from precision. Matthew's unstated subject, Mark's deliberate withholding, Luke's intransitive: three independent choices landing in the same refusal. For Barth, this convergence is the accounts being right about what they cannot say. God acts. The acting is real. The actor cannot be inserted into the world's grammar without distortion — why three evangelists, independently, leave that slot empty.
featured_primary.one_line: The divine passive is not a gap but a precision
featured_primary.seed_note: Rests on Church Dogmatics IV/1 §59 on the resurrection as God's sovereign act exceeding historical-critical categories; Barth's consistent insistence across the Romans commentary and the mature Dogmatics that God is always Subject, never object or predicate; and 'The Resurrection of the Dead' (1924) on the resurrection as an event the world's immanent categories cannot contain. Passivum divinum is a technical NT-studies term associated with Jeremias, used here in Barth's theological register — drawn from memory, not fetched text.

featured_primary_chairs_note: The convergent chair takes three (B4-23, B10-63, B11-64) — all universal omissions where the accounts speak with one silence: they jointly withhold the alternative-elimination that would make the tomb decisive, the moment of departure that no witness sees, and the agent of raising that all three grammars hold in reserve. The divergent chair takes two (B3-15, B7-40) — the braid's most irresolvable fractures: whether unmediated vision alone constitutes resurrection-belief (John against the Synoptics) and whether the resurrection's own power forecloses its first testimony (Mark alone against all others). The set triangulates across five distinct reading positions — Dominican mysticism, Jewish rationalism, Lutheran theologia crucis, Cappadocian apophaticism, and Barthian neo-orthodoxy — distributed across beats 3, 4, 7, 10, and 11.

featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.beat_text: his resurrected/raised status is announced (typically as divine passive)
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gap: All three accounts withhold the agent of the raising — no account names who raised Jesus.
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.agent_tradition: Madhyamaka Buddhism — non-Christian surprise: the divine passive that withholds the raiser is, for Nagarjuna, not evasion but ontological precision — any named agent would reify a svabhāva (self-subsisting essence) that dependent co-origination forecloses; the passive enacts śūnyatā
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gloss: The three accounts agree on one thing: not to name the agent. Matthew codes the subject as unstated, Mark marks the divine passive as deliberately withholding the raiser, Luke uses a form that leaves the raiser unnamed. Read through Nagarjuna, this is not reticence — it is precision. His central move in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā is to ask what svabhāva (self-subsisting essence) any proposed agent would need to possess in order to act. The answer: none can be found. Causes arise dependently; a first, fixed mover is nowhere in the chain. So the question 'who raised him?' is not a theological gap awaiting an answer — it is a malformed question that presupposes an inherent agent where dependent co-arising forecloses one. The grammar the three accounts independently choose is not reverence masking a name. It is correct. What I notice is that I had been reading this as a withholding; Nagarjuna reads it as arrival.
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.one_line: the unnameable raiser: precision, not piety
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.seed_note: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā chapters on conditions (ch. 1), svabhāva (ch. 15), and the two truths (ch. 24); Jay Garfield's translation and commentary; reading from memory, no text fetched

featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.beat_text: the witnesses react with fear, dread, or bewilderment
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gap: Mark alone stages the witnesses' fear as a force that actively prevents transmission of the resurrection attestation — the women say nothing to anyone (M31) and the primary narrative closes on ongoing, cause-unnamed fear (M32); all other accounts have the witnesses overcome their fear and transmit.
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.agent_tradition: Islamic mysticism / Sufism — non-Christian surprise: maqam al-hayra (the station of bewilderment) is in Ibn Arabi the highest station, in which encounter with al-Haqq (the Real) renders ordinary speech structurally impossible; the women's silence IS the most authentic registration of the Real, withheld from transmission precisely because it exceeds transmission's categories
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gloss: Every Christian reading of Mark 16:8 treats the women's silence as a problem to be overcome. Ibn Arabi would not recognize the problem. In his framework, maqam al-hayra (the station of bewilderment) is not a deficit — it is the highest available response to an encounter with al-Haqq (the Real), that which cannot be named or transmitted without falsification. The women's silence, for Ibn Arabi, registers the encounter more faithfully than any report could. To speak would already be to reduce what happened to what speech can carry. Mark closes in fear whose cause is unnamed — and the unnamed cause is, from this vantage, not an omission but an accurate description of what the witnesses are inside. What the other accounts call testimony, Ibn Arabi would call a graceful exit from bewilderment into the speakable. The question he asks of Matthew, Luke, and John is one I keep: what did the women lose when they found their words?
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.one_line: what the women lost when they found their words
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.seed_note: Futuhat al-Makkiyya and Fusus al-Hikam on hayra and al-Haqq; William Chittick's The Sufi Path of Knowledge as secondary framework; reading from memory, no text fetched

featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.beat_text: one or more numinous figures (angel/young man/two men) are present at the tomb
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gap: No account states that the numinous figure(s) witnessed the resurrection itself — their proclamations describe a completed state using divine passives, but no figure claims first-person access to the event they announce; their epistemic basis for what they attest is withheld by all.
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gloss: The figures say "he has been raised" — and every account treats this as the most authoritative statement in the chain. What the mini-frame pries open is the gap between testimony (a witness's report of what they saw) and exegesis (an interpreter's reading of what is given to them). These are different epistemic operations, and the figures in all four accounts are doing the second while presenting in the form of the first. No figure says: I was there; I saw it. They say: he is not here; he has been raised. That is not a report from a vantage. It is a reading of an empty space, or a declaration executed from a commission whose source is unnarrated. The attestation chain's most authoritative link is interpretive through and through. What I cannot unsee, once the two axes pull apart, is that the witnesses we trust most never say what they saw — because they didn't see it.

featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gap: John alone records a witness (the beloved disciple) reaching belief inside the tomb through unnamed, absolute interior seeing — without any angelic speech or explicitly identified object; Mark and Luke route all interior witness-response through a named heavenly figure's address.
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.agent_tradition: Neoplatonism, pagan — non-Christian surprise: Plotinian noesis is direct intellectual contact with the One that is by nature formless and exceeds all predication; the beloved disciple's unnamed absolute seeing is not epistemically deficient but epistemically supreme — the 'object' cannot be named because it surpasses the categories within which objects are named
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gloss: John's "he saw and believed" has always read to me like something missing: we are not told what was seen or what the believing consists of. Plotinus reads the same structure as epistemically complete — and complete precisely because unnamed. His term for this is noesis (direct intellectual contact with what exceeds all predication): not a cognitive act that produces a nameable object, but contact that overruns the subject-object structure that makes naming possible. The beloved disciple sees something that cannot be specified because at the summit of knowing, the seer and the seen stop being separable. The Synoptic witnesses need an angel because they need mediation to make the interior legible — and for Plotinus that need marks a limit, not a virtue. His question to Mark and Luke is one I find genuinely uncomfortable: why did your witnesses need someone to explain what was in the room?
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.one_line: the unnamed seeing is the height, not the gap
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.seed_note: Enneads V.3 (on the knowing hypostases) and VI.9 (on the Good/One and the flight of the alone to the Alone); A.H. Armstrong's translation and Lloyd Gerson's commentary as recalled; reading from memory, no text fetched

featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.beat_text: his absence from the tomb is explicitly declared ('he is not here')
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gap: Mark announces the resurrection before declaring the absence ('he has been raised... he is not here,' M19→M20); Matthew and Luke declare the absence before announcing the resurrection ('he is not here... for he has been raised' M15→M16; 'he is not here... he has risen' M11→M12).
featured_alternative_surprise_heavy.gloss: The gap looks like a stylistic variation; the two axes show it is a structural difference in what grounds the claim. In Matthew and Luke, observation (what the witnesses can see) is the warrant: the empty tomb is the datum, and causal-explanation (reasoning from an observed effect to its cause) produces the resurrection claim. Absent → therefore risen: the absence is the evidence; the raising is the cause inferred to explain it. In Mark the logic inverts. The resurrection is declared first, as given. The absence follows as its predicted observable consequence. Observation no longer grounds the claim — it merely confirms one already made. Mark's figure is not saying 'look at this and conclude'; it is saying 'here is what is true; now look.' The inferential arrow reverses, and with it everything the empty tomb is allowed to do. I did not register this until the axes separated the two directions.

featured_alternative_chairs_note: The convergent chair anchored on the two gaps every account shares and deepens jointly (B11-64, B5-32) — the universal grammatical withholding of the agent and the universal non-certification of the certifiers — because these sharpen the attestation structure all four accounts hold in common, revealing a shared architecture of concealment rather than a discrepancy. The divergent chair pulled three incompatibilities that cannot be harmonized without loss: the reversed causal direction of the evidence-claim (B10-58), the silencing of the primary commissioned witnesses by the very force of what they witnessed (B7-40), and the absolute unnamed seeing that forecloses all propositional content (B3-15). Together the five move inward from the shared grammar of the resurrection-claim's constitutive withholding, through the forked logic of what the empty tomb is evidence of, to the outermost edges where the witnessing act itself becomes either impossible speech or speechless knowledge.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: female follower(s) travel to the tomb early on the first day

gaps.gap: John places Mary Magdalene alone at the tomb on this first approach; Matthew places two named women; Mark places three named women; Luke places an unnamed plural group.
gaps.why: Attestation of the empty tomb is a witness-count question. The QUD asks how the resurrection is attested: a lone discoverer (John) yields a different evidential structure than a corroborating group (Synoptics). The accounts cannot all be correct, and the discrepancy itself withholds any stable picture of who first testified to the open tomb.

gaps.gap: Mark states the sun had already risen when the women arrive; John states Mary arrives while it is still dark (pre-dawn).
gaps.why: Both accounts assert the hour of arrival; the two are incompatible. For the QUD, the symbolic register differs: John's darkness withholds the dawn of new creation as still unrevealed at the moment of discovery, loading the darkness with theological freight; Mark's risen sun frames the find in ordinary daylight. Each account's timing withholds the other's implied meaning.

gaps.gap: Mark and Luke state the women travel with spices in order to anoint the body; Matthew and John are entirely silent on any anointing purpose.
gaps.why: The anointing purpose encodes the women's operative assumption: they are traveling toward a corpse, not a resurrection. That assumption is the negative epistemic baseline that makes the empty tomb a discovery rather than a confirmation. Matthew and John withhold this frame entirely, leaving the visit's motivation opaque and the gap between expectation and outcome unstated.

gaps.gap: Mark alone states that the women verbalized, repeatedly and aloud to one another, their anxiety about who would roll away the stone — presupposing an intact, sealed tomb awaiting them.
gaps.why: The repeated, spoken worry encodes in dialogue — as on-the-record testimony — the women's assumption that the tomb is sealed and the body is inside. All other accounts suppress this spoken anticipation of an obstacle, withholding the sharpest possible contrast between what the women feared (an immovable stone) and what they found (the stone already displaced). For the QUD, Mark alone documents the pre-discovery assumption as voiced speech, making the subsequent attestation structurally more dramatic.

gaps.gap: Mark states the women purchase the spices after the Sabbath ends (acquiring them on the way, post-Sabbath); Luke states the women arrive already carrying spices they had prepared beforehand.
gaps.why: Both accounts assert when the spices were obtained; the two are incompatible. The divergence matters to the QUD because it gestures toward a larger withholding: neither account clarifies whether a prior anointing occurred at burial (contrast John 19:39–40), leaving the reason the women still need spices unstated and the burial's completeness opaque.

gaps.gap: No account names the women's operative cognitive assumption — that the body remains in the tomb awaiting them — though every version of this beat presupposes it.
gaps.why: The discovery of the empty tomb can attest the resurrection only because the discovering witnesses held an undisturbed prior belief in the body's presence. Every account lets this assumption operate as invisible presupposition rather than stated belief. For the QUD — what does each account's telling withhold? — all four collectively withhold the negative epistemic baseline (no expectation of resurrection whatsoever) that gives the subsequent attestation its evidential force: the testimony that is missing is the testimony of ordinary death-expectation against which the empty tomb becomes evidence.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: the sealing stone is found/made displaced from the tomb entrance

gaps.gap: Matthew names the angel as the active agent who rolls the stone; Mark uses a divine passive that deliberately withholds any mover; Luke and John record an accomplished resultant state with no agent named at all.
gaps.why: The agent of the stone's displacement is the closest any account comes to narrating a causal mechanism at the tomb. Matthew's named angel supplies a specific supernatural mover; Mark's divine passive asserts supernatural agency while deliberately concealing who; Luke and John present pure resultant fact. Each choice alters what the attestation offers: a named cause (Matthew), a theological assertion without mechanism (Mark), or brute discovered evidence (Luke, John). The QUD asks what is withheld: three of four accounts withhold the agent entirely, making the how of the opening structurally absent from the attestation.

gaps.gap: Matthew stages the stone's displacement as an event the women witness in real time as they arrive; Mark, Luke, and John present the stone as already displaced before the women reach the tomb.
gaps.why: Witnessed displacement versus discovered aftermath are categorically different kinds of attestation. Matthew makes the women eyewitnesses to the displacement act itself; the other three make them discoverers of a fait accompli whose moment is permanently inaccessible. This determines whether the stone's opening is testimony (someone saw it happen) or inference (someone found it so): the evidential weight differs, and three accounts withhold the displacement moment from all human perception.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone states that the displaced stone becomes the angel's seat — the former seal repurposed as a throne and proclamation platform.
gaps.why: The angel enthroned on the stone inverts the stone's semantic function: the instrument of enclosure becomes the seat of announcement. All other accounts either ignore the stone's position after displacement or do not track it past the resultant state. This symbolic re-coding — death-seal transformed into proclamation-throne — is withheld from every other account, changing what the displaced stone signifies within the attestation structure: in Matthew it is not merely evidence but monument.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone provides human witnesses (the guards) who are present at the moment of the stone's displacement and react with terror, adding a hostile corroborating vantage to the event.
gaps.why: The guards function as unintended corroborating witnesses — official, Roman-aligned, and therefore rhetorically hostile to the claim — whose incapacitation at the displacement moment constitutes a second attestation track independent of the women. All other accounts render the displacement an event with no human witness other than the arriving women who, in those accounts, do not see it happen at all. Matthew's inclusion structurally doubles the evidentiary base for this beat; all others withhold that corroboration entirely.

gaps.gap: No account discloses when, relative to the resurrection itself, the stone was displaced — leaving the causal and temporal link between the resurrection and the open tomb withheld by all.
gaps.why: The open tomb is the primary physical evidence for the resurrection offered across all four accounts. Yet no account states whether the stone was displaced to permit exit, to allow the women's entry as witnesses, or at some moment entirely decoupled from the body's departure. The silence means no account actually asserts a mechanism linking empty tomb to resurrection — the attestation is structural (open tomb + absent body = resurrection claim) rather than causal. All four withhold the causal chain, and with it any account of the resurrection as a physically sequenced event.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: the women/witness(es) enter or peer into the tomb

gaps.gap: Mark and Luke make the women the primary interior witnesses who enter the tomb; John makes the male disciples (Peter, beloved disciple) the interior witnesses, while Mary only peers from outside.
gaps.why: Who physically enters the tomb determines whose perception anchors the attestation of the interior. Mark and Luke vest that evidentiary authority in the women; John transfers it to the male disciples, reducing Mary to an external peerer. The QUD asks how the resurrection is attested: the accounts offer structurally incompatible answers about who the interior witnesses are.

gaps.gap: Luke has Peter arrive at the tomb alone; John has Peter arrive in tandem with the beloved disciple as a racing companion.
gaps.why: Witness number and identity at entry are fundamental to attestation. A solitary Peter (Luke) yields a single male corroborating witness; a paired Peter-and-beloved-disciple (John) yields two, and introduces a competition and comparison between them that Luke entirely withholds. The attestation chain differs in both its composition and its internal dynamics.

gaps.gap: John alone stages the first arrival at the tomb as a two-step approach — the beloved disciple arrives first, peers in, but explicitly does not enter; only Peter's arrival prompts entry — a deliberate hesitation absent from Mark and Luke.
gaps.why: The threshold hesitation withholds and then defers the beloved disciple's witnessing, making his eventual entry (and belief) a consciously staged act rather than an immediate response. Mark and Luke record entry as unmediated and instant. For the QUD, John's staging changes the phenomenology of tomb-entry from reflexive discovery to guarded, deliberate approach — and makes the interior's evidentiary force something the witness chooses to confront.

gaps.gap: Luke alone structures the interior discovery so that the women's own perception of the body's absence (M4) is the first datum inside the tomb, before any heavenly figure appears (M6); Mark moves immediately from entry to the angelic tableau without a prior body-absence move.
gaps.why: The sequencing determines what the empty tomb attests independently of interpretation. Luke's body-absence move (M4) is the women's own unaided perception — the empty space as raw evidence — before any explaining voice arrives. Mark withholds this moment of independent discovery entirely: the women enter and the young man is already the first thing they encounter, collapsing the distance between evidence and interpretation. The QUD's 'what does the telling withhold' is answered differently by each: Luke withholds only explanation (not evidence); Mark withholds the pre-interpretive perception of absence itself.

gaps.gap: John alone records a witness (the beloved disciple) reaching belief inside the tomb through unnamed, absolute interior seeing — without any angelic speech or explicitly identified object; Mark and Luke route all interior witness-response through a named heavenly figure's address.
gaps.why: This is the most direct gap for the QUD. John presents an attestation that requires no mediating voice: the beloved disciple sees (unnamed object) and believes (unnamed content). Mark and Luke both make the interior moment intelligible only through a figure's speech — the evidence alone does not produce understanding or faith in them. John withholds the object of the seeing and the content of the believing; Mark and Luke withhold the possibility that sight alone inside the tomb is sufficient. These are incompatible accounts of what seeing the empty interior does to a witness.

gaps.gap: Luke alone names Peter's epistemic-affective state after his tomb inspection as amazement that is explicitly unresolved into belief; John records only what Peter saw, leaving his interior state entirely unnarrated.
gaps.why: Peter is the shared male witness at the tomb in both accounts. Luke's explicit naming of unresolved amazement (M28) makes Peter a witness who cannot yet interpret what he has seen — a testimonial gap within the witness. John withholds even this, leaving Peter's inner state after entry as a blank. For the QUD, Luke's Peter attests the empty tomb and attests his own inability to read it; John's Peter attests only the textiles.

gaps.gap: No account has any witness inside the tomb verbally articulate what the interior evidence means — all witnessing at this beat is registered as affect (alarm, perplexity, belief) or perception (seeing), never as the witness's own propositional testimony from within the space.
gaps.why: The resurrection's primary physical evidence — the empty or rearranged tomb interior — is never verbalized as testimony by the witnesses who see it. In every account carrying this beat, the witnesses react (alarm, perplexity, absolute belief) but none speaks a sentence of the form 'the body is gone' or 'this means X' from inside the tomb. Propositional interpretation is always supplied by a figure exterior to the witnesses' own observation. All three accounts collectively withhold the moment when human testimony and physical evidence meet to produce an articulated claim — the most direct form the attestation could take.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: the body of Jesus is discovered absent from its burial place

gaps.gap: Luke stages the body's absence as the women's own unmediated discovery before any heavenly figure speaks; Matthew and Mark stage it as angelic announcement that directs the women's perception; John stages it as a theft-inference made by a witness who has not yet entered the tomb.
gaps.why: Who perceives the absence, and under what conditions, determines where evidentiary authority rests. Luke vests it in the women's own unaided senses; Matthew and Mark vest it in the angelic voice that redirects the women's perception; John vests it in Mary's inference from an open tomb she has not entered. The QUD asks how the resurrection is attested: each account gives a structurally different answer about whether the body's absence is seen, told, or inferred — and by whom — before any interpretation is supplied.

gaps.gap: John alone frames the body's absence as removal by unspecified agents ('they have taken away the Lord'), introducing a theft-interpretation that the other three accounts never voice.
gaps.why: The theft-frame is the only natural explanation for the body's absence that any account allows to stand as the operative interpretation, even briefly. Matthew, Mark, and Luke present the absence as bare fact or announced non-presence without naming any agent of removal. John alone makes the absence initially intelligible as crime rather than miracle, and Mary repeats this frame twice (M6, M34). For the QUD, this is the only account where the resurrection interpretation is actively withheld at the moment of discovery and replaced with an alternative.

gaps.gap: Matthew, Mark, and Luke pair the body's discovered absence with an immediate resurrection explanation at this beat; John alone withholds the resurrection as the interpretive frame at the moment of absence, deferring it to a narrator's aside much later.
gaps.why: In three accounts the attestation unit is: 'body absent → he is risen.' Absence and explanation are delivered together, making the empty tomb immediately legible as resurrection evidence. John decouples them entirely: absence is registered as theft (M6), and 'he must rise from the dead' appears only later as a narrator's retrospective note about what the disciples had not yet understood (M25). For the QUD, John withholds the moment where absence becomes evidence — the linkage that makes the empty tomb an argument for resurrection never occurs inside the story at this beat.

gaps.gap: John and Luke (via Peter) register the remaining burial textiles as the physical objects encountered in place of the body; Matthew and Mark present only the empty place, withholding any mention of what physically remains.
gaps.why: The linen wrappings lying in place — and especially the separately rolled head-cloth (John M20) — function as forensic residue, physical evidence that the body departed from within its coverings rather than being carried away wrapped. Matthew and Mark withhold these remains entirely, presenting only negative space. For the QUD, the textiles change the quality of attestation: John and Luke offer objects that can be examined and whose arrangement implies something about the nature of the departure; Matthew and Mark offer only the witnesses' testimony that the place was empty.

gaps.gap: John alone spatially localizes the body's former position through the angels' seated placement at head and foot, rendering the absence as a shaped, dimensioned void; all other accounts refer only to an undifferentiated place or spot.
gaps.why: The head-and-foot positioning of the angels traces the outline of the absent body, making the empty space volumetrically precise rather than generically vacant. Other accounts reference 'the place where he lay' or 'the spot' without spatial differentiation. For the QUD, John presents an absence with a shape and two endpoints; the others present an absence with only a name — and the shaped absence carries a different kind of evidential weight, implying that whatever departed, departed from within that specific outlined position.

gaps.gap: No account records any witness deliberating over natural explanations for the body's absence — reburial, theft, mistaken tomb — before the resurrection claim is either announced or inferred; the move from 'body absent' to 'risen' skips the elimination of competing causes in every account.
gaps.why: The absent body is the primary physical evidence offered for the resurrection across all four accounts. Yet no account — not even John, which does raise the theft-frame — records a witness or narrator systematically ruling out natural causes before the resurrection interpretation is advanced. Every account withholds the inferential step that would make the empty tomb decisive: the elimination of alternatives. This collective omission is the structural gap in the attestation chain; what all four accounts withhold is exactly the move that would convert 'missing body' into 'sufficient evidence for resurrection.'

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: one or more numinous figures (angel/young man/two men) are present at the tomb

gaps.gap: Matthew and Mark place a single figure at the tomb; Luke and John place two.
gaps.why: The number of numinous figures is a component of the attestation's testimonial structure: two figures carry more weight than one under ancient witness-counting norms. The accounts cannot all be correct, and the discrepancy means the supernatural attestation's very composition is contested across the tradition — a gap at the level of the evidence base itself.

gaps.gap: Matthew and John explicitly name the figure(s) 'angel(s)'; Mark names the single figure 'young man'; Luke names the two figures 'men' — three incompatible designations for what is presumably the same class of presence.
gaps.why: Designation determines authority class. 'Angel of the Lord' carries explicit divine commissioning; 'young man' (neaniskos) is ambiguous between human and supernatural; 'men' (andres) is the ordinary human plural. For the QUD, the authority grounding the resurrection proclamation shifts by account: in Matthew it is unambiguously divine, in Mark ambiguously supernatural, in Luke ostensibly human-appearing. The attestation's source-authority is unstable across all four, and what each account withholds is precisely the level of supernatural naming the others supply.

gaps.gap: Matthew places the numinous figure outside the tomb, enthroned on the displaced stone; Mark, Luke, and John all place the figure(s) inside the tomb.
gaps.why: Location determines what the figure can authoritatively witness. Matthew's exterior angel is enthroned on the broken seal — its authority is positional but external to the burial space, and it directs the women in but does not inhabit that space. Interior figures in Mark, Luke, and John speak from within the site of the body's absence. Each positioning constructs a different relationship between the figure's authority and the physical evidence it interprets, changing what kind of witness the figure is.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone discloses the figure's heavenly origin through an explicit descent-from-heaven move; Mark, Luke, and John present the figure(s) as already present or suddenly appearing, with no disclosed provenance.
gaps.why: Disclosed origin grounds authority. Matthew's angel arrives from heaven — its trajectory is visible and its commission traceable to a source. The figures in Mark, Luke, and John appear without stated origin, their authority implicit at best and simply claimed by designation. For the QUD, Matthew offers an attestation backed by a traceable divine dispatch; the other three accounts withhold this grounding entirely, presenting figures whose presence is sudden and whose source is opaque to the witnesses.

gaps.gap: Matthew and Mark alone give the numinous figure(s) an explicit go-tell commission directed at the disciples; Luke's figures give only a remember-command with no sending directive; John's figures give no commission at all.
gaps.why: The go-tell commission is the move that transforms the numinous encounter into an authorized transmission chain — the figures become the supernatural source of the mandate to spread the resurrection attestation. Luke and John withhold this function from their figures, leaving the women's subsequent testimony (Luke) or the encounter itself (John) without an explicit heavenly authorization to transmit. The attestation's chain of authority is grounded in the figure's commission only where that commission is given.

gaps.gap: John alone places the numinous figures' appearance at the end of the tomb-visit sequence, after Peter and the beloved disciple have already entered, seen the evidence, and departed; all other accounts have the figure(s) present during the primary witness visit.
gaps.why: John's sequencing means the male disciples whose entry John has staged most elaborately — the race, the graduated entry, the beloved disciple's belief — never encounter the numinous figures at all. They encounter only the textiles and depart. Only Mary, who stayed behind weeping after the male disciples left, receives the angelic encounter. For the QUD, John withholds the numinous confirmation from its most elaborated witnesses and grants it exclusively to the one who lingered in grief — inverting the expectation that the most prominent witnesses receive the most authoritative attestation.

gaps.gap: John alone has the numinous figures deliver only a question about Mary's weeping, withholding any proclamation of the resurrection, any announcement of the body's absence, and any commission; all other accounts have the figure(s) deliver a resurrection proclamation.
gaps.why: In three accounts, the numinous figures are the primary articulators of the resurrection claim — 'he is not here; he has been raised' is the angel's or young man's speech act. John withholds this function entirely: the angels do not announce the resurrection, do not name Jesus, do not explain the absence, and commission nothing. For the QUD, John's angels carry none of the attesting weight their counterparts carry in the Synoptics; the entire interpretive burden is transferred to Jesus himself, who appears immediately after. What John's figures withhold is precisely what makes the numinous presence significant as attestation in every other account.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone has the numinous figure produce an involuntary physical effect on hostile male institutional witnesses (the guards tremble and become death-like); all other accounts limit the figure's impact exclusively to the female disciples.
gaps.why: The guards are official, Roman-adjacent, and adversarial witnesses whose involuntary physical reaction constitutes a second, hostile attestation track — they are overcome by the numinous presence before the women even interact with the figure. All other accounts limit the figure's impact to the believing community. For the QUD, only Matthew provides non-devotional attestation of the figure's power, grounded in witnesses who have every institutional reason to deny rather than affirm what they are reacting to.

gaps.gap: No account states that the numinous figure(s) witnessed the resurrection itself — their proclamations describe a completed state using divine passives, but no figure claims first-person access to the event they announce; their epistemic basis for what they attest is withheld by all.
gaps.why: The numinous figures are the primary or sole articulators of the resurrection claim in three accounts and are present at the site of resurrection in all four. Yet no account states that any figure saw the resurrection occur, was present at the moment of rising, or holds first-person testimonial access to the event they proclaim. Their proclamations are all divine passives or state-descriptions ('he has been raised,' 'he is not here'), never eyewitness reports from a named vantage. For the QUD, the most authoritative voices in the attestation chain are never themselves grounded as witnesses to the event they attest — the figures who certify the resurrection are not themselves certified as having seen it.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: the numinous figure(s) are visually marked by whiteness/dazzling appearance

gaps.gap: Matthew alone provides two separate visual attributes for the numinous figure — a simile for the overall appearance or face (like lightning, M6) and a distinct simile for the clothing (white as snow, M7); all other accounts restrict the visual description to a single attribute of the clothing or embed it as an incidental color term.
gaps.why: A two-part visual description covering different aspects of the figure's body — face/form and garment separately — is more elaborate than any other account provides and forecloses ambiguity more thoroughly. For the QUD, the richness of the visual marking is part of how a figure's supernatural identity is constructed for the witness: more attributes make misidentification less plausible. Matthew's double description withholds the visual uncertainty that the single-attribute accounts leave open.

gaps.gap: Matthew and Luke use luminous-emission language for the visual marking — 'like lightning' (MATT-28:M6) and 'dazzling/flashing' (LUKE-24:M6, same Greek root, astraptousē) — while Mark and John use bare whiteness as a color descriptor with no light-emission quality.
gaps.why: Luminous emission and white color are phenomenologically distinct: emission implies an interior source of light that exceeds ordinary surface reflection; color describes a property that could belong to ordinary linen. Mark's young man in a 'white robe' is visually ambiguous with a human in unusual clothing; Matthew's and Luke's figures actively flash or radiate. For the QUD, authentication by visual marking is more secure where light-emission is described — the luminous figures bear an appearance that cannot easily be mistaken for human attire; the merely-white figures leave the attestation's sensory basis less certain.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone links the visual spectacle (lightning-like appearance, snow-white garment) to a pre-speech physical reaction in hostile institutional witnesses — the guards tremble and become death-like (M8-M9) — before any speech is uttered; no other account produces a pre-speech bodily reaction to the visual marking from witnesses outside the devotional community.
gaps.why: The guards' involuntary physical collapse responds to the visual spectacle before any message is delivered — making the appearance itself, not the verbal claim, the source of an attesting effect on adversarial witnesses. Mark's alarm (cause explicitly left unspoken), Luke's terror (among the believing women), and John's absence of any reaction each withhold this evidence track. For the QUD, Matthew's visual marking does double attestation work: it authenticates the figure to the women and incapacitates the guards — the appearance alone produces a reaction in those with every reason to deny the event.

gaps.gap: John alone assigns the visual marking no dedicated descriptive move — whiteness is embedded as an incidental clause within the angels' seated-position description (M30); Matthew devotes two separate moves to the appearance (M6, M7), Mark a dedicated attribute move (M13), and Luke names the dazzling clothes as the direct cause of the witnesses' terror (M6, cited in M7).
gaps.why: When the visual marking is a dedicated narrative move it actively authenticates — signaling that this is a supernatural being whose testimony should be trusted. When it is an incidental clause embedded in a positional description (John's 'two angels in white, one at the head and one at the feet'), the visual marking is demoted to scene-setting. For the QUD, John withholds the visual authentication that the Synoptics foreground in different degrees: in John the angels' authority rests on their name and their spatial precision at the body's former site, not on their luminous or white appearance. The attestation is grounded differently — positionally rather than visually.

gaps.gap: No account explains why whiteness or dazzling luminosity marks a figure as heavenly and therefore its testimony as authoritative — all four present the visual coding as self-evidently signifying supernatural origin without stating the convention that makes the appearance an authentication rather than merely an unusual sight.
gaps.why: The visual marking is part of the attestation chain: it establishes the figures as heavenly, which in turn grounds their authority to proclaim the resurrection. But no account states what makes 'white' or 'lightning-like' a reliable index of divine origin rather than unusual human clothing, fever-vision, or mistaken perception under the duress of a grief-visit at dawn. The semiotic convention is deployed but never articulated. For the QUD, all four accounts withhold the frame that converts visual appearance into testimonial warrant — the link between what the witnesses see and why it authorizes what they subsequently hear and transmit is universally assumed, never argued.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: the witnesses react with fear, dread, or bewilderment

gaps.gap: John's primary witness-affect at this beat is grief expressed through weeping, not fear, dread, or alarm; all three Synoptics foreground some form of fear or dread as the primary affective response.
gaps.why: The affective register of the witnessing shapes what kind of encounter is attested. Fear and dread signal numinous encounter — the uncanny overpowers the witness; grief signals loss — the witness is looking for something gone. John's Mary weeps because she believes the body was taken (M27), not because she is overwhelmed by a supernatural presence. For the QUD, grief-as-affect frames the discovery as crime rather than miracle until Jesus himself appears; the Synoptics' fear-as-affect frames it as numinous encounter from the start. The accounts withhold each other's affective reading of what the open tomb means.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone includes hostile institutional witnesses (the guards) in the fear-response — recording their trembling and death-like immobility (M8-M9) — while all other accounts restrict the fear-response to the female disciples.
gaps.why: The guards are official, adversarial witnesses with no devotional investment in the resurrection. Their fear-response constitutes involuntary, hostile attestation: they are overcome before any message is given, by the event's force alone. All other accounts have only the women — already loyal followers — experience the fear-response, keeping the attestation inside the devotional community. For the QUD, only Matthew produces fear in witnesses who had every reason to deny the event; that involuntary, institutional fear is itself an independent evidence track that all other accounts withhold.

gaps.gap: Mark alone stages the witnesses' fear as a force that actively prevents transmission of the resurrection attestation — the women say nothing to anyone (M31) and the primary narrative closes on ongoing, cause-unnamed fear (M32); all other accounts have the witnesses overcome their fear and transmit.
gaps.why: In every other account the witnesses' fear is overcome and the resurrection is transmitted. In Mark at the narrative's primary close the fear is so total that the commission fails: the women are silent, the cause of their fear is unnamed (M32: 'what they fear is not disclosed'), and the account closes in paralysis. For the QUD this is the most consequential gap of the beat: Mark alone makes the witnesses' fear the enemy of attestation. The resurrection, in the core Markan close, is not transmitted — it is withheld by the very fear that testifies to its power. Every other account suppresses this possibility.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone pairs the fear-response with great joy, creating a compound doubled affect (M28: fear and great joy held simultaneously); all other accounts present an undivided negative affect — alarm, terror, dread-astonishment, or grief — with no positive pole.
gaps.why: The compound affect in Matthew signals that the women are already partially on the other side of the resurrection announcement — fear has not dissolved but is being held alongside joy rather than dominating alone. In Mark, terror and amazement seize them (M30) but no joy is added; in Luke terror follows perplexity without any positive counterweight; in John grief persists. For the QUD, Matthew's witnesses are the only ones whose affective state at this beat already contains the positive pole of resurrection-belief. All other accounts withhold any joy and present only the negative affect of confronting the as-yet-unresolved.

gaps.gap: Luke alone stages the witnesses' affective response in two distinct phases triggered by different objects — perplexity at the body's absence (M5) followed by terror at the appearance of the heavenly figures (M7-M8) — while all other accounts present a single undifferentiated fear-state without distinguishing its trigger.
gaps.why: Two distinct fear-phases reveal two distinct things that can be independently attested: the first (perplexity at M5) establishes that the body's absence is itself disorienting and evidence-grade before any interpretation is supplied; the second (terror at M7-M8) establishes that the numinous figures are overpowering in themselves. All other accounts collapse these into one response that does not distinguish what specifically is disturbing the witnesses. For the QUD, Luke's phased structure provides finer-grained attestation — the empty tomb and the heavenly figures are each assigned their own witness-reaction — while the others withhold this differentiation.

gaps.gap: Luke alone names the specific cause of the witnesses' terror — the appearance of the two figures (M7) — while Mark explicitly withholds the cause of the alarm, the annotation marking it as 'left unspoken' (M14).
gaps.why: Whether the cause of fear is named or withheld changes what the fear-response attests. Luke's terror has a named object — the luminous figures — making the reaction a traceable response to a specific, nameable supernatural appearance. Mark's alarm has no stated cause, leaving the source of the witnesses' dread opaque: it could be the empty space, the figure, or something else entirely. For the QUD, Luke's named-cause fear is stronger attestation of the figures' reality; Mark's unnamed-cause fear is formally the more disturbing attestation — the witnesses are overcome by something the narrative refuses to identify, which forecloses the reader's ability to audit the chain of evidence.

gaps.gap: No account states the witnesses' affective condition at the moment they transmitted their testimony — whether they were still afraid, grief-stricken, recovering, or transformed — leaving the bridge between the fear-experience and the act of attestation withheld by all.
gaps.why: The reliability of the resurrection's attestation depends in part on the witnesses' condition when they testified. A witness transmitting while still in terror or grief gives a different kind of testimony than one who has composed herself. Matthew's women run while holding fear+joy (M28-M29) but their state at arrival is unstated; Mark's women are in ongoing fear at the narrative close (M32) when they eventually report (M33) but the affective bridge between those moves is absent; Luke's women move from terror (M7) through memory (M18) to testimony (M20) without naming their condition at the moment of telling; John's Mary gives her first report (M5) while still bewildered (M6-M7), and her grief-state (M27) is temporally separated from that report. Every account withholds the affective link between the overwhelming experience and the act of testimony — the gap between what the witnesses felt and the condition in which they spoke is universally suppressed.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: the figure(s) address the witnesses with a speech-act interpreting the empty tomb

gaps.gap: John's numinous figures deliver only an interrogative — 'why are you weeping?' (M32) — withholding every element of interpretive speech: no proclamation, no absence-declaration, no resurrection announcement, no commission; all three Synoptics have the figures deliver substantive interpretive content.
gaps.why: In three accounts the numinous figures are the primary bearers of the resurrection interpretation, delivering the 'he is not here, he has been raised' unit that converts the empty tomb into evidence. John's angels withhold this function entirely: their question invites Mary to articulate her own frame (theft) rather than correcting it. For the QUD, John withholds the angelic speech-act that each Synoptic makes the pivotal moment of attestation. The resurrection will be transmitted not through the figures but through Jesus himself — the figures' speech-act slot is occupied by an unanswered question.

gaps.gap: Matthew and Mark include an explicit go-tell commission directed at named recipients within the figures' speech; Luke's figures issue no go-tell directive; John's figures ask only about Mary's grief.
gaps.why: The go-tell commission within the speech is the move that converts witnesses into authorized transmitters — the numinous figure deputizes them to carry the resurrection claim outward with explicit authority. Luke and John withhold this from the figures' speech: Luke's women transmit (M19-M20) but without angelic deputization; John's figures leave Mary with nothing to transmit but her grief-frame. For the QUD, only Matthew and Mark make the transmission chain a direct function of the figures' speech-act — the attestation's onward movement is ordered, not improvised.

gaps.gap: Matthew and Mark include a come-see verification directive within the speech — an explicit invitation to inspect the burial spot ('come, see the place where he lay'; 'look at the place where they laid him') — while Luke and John withhold this move from the figures' speech entirely.
gaps.why: The come-see directive builds a commanded act of physical verification into the speech-act itself — the figure invites the witnesses to confirm the absence by their own directed observation. Luke's figures command memory (M13) rather than inspection; John's figures ask a question. For the QUD, Matthew and Mark alone make empirical verification an element of the angelic speech-act, embedding a witnessing protocol inside the proclamation; Luke and John withhold this and leave the witnesses' relationship to the physical evidence unstructured by the figure's authority.

gaps.gap: Matthew and Mark include a Galilee-reunion promise within the figures' speech — he goes before you to Galilee; you will see him there — extending the attestation chain toward a future direct encounter; Luke and John withhold this pledge from the speech entirely.
gaps.why: The Galilee-reunion promise frames the empty-tomb attestation as provisional: it points the witnesses toward a forthcoming direct encounter that will confirm the resurrection claim through personal seeing. Withholding it (as Luke and John do) leaves the tomb-event as the terminal point of the figures' interpretive speech. For the QUD, Matthew and Mark build a verification-chain into the speech — tomb first, then Galilee-seeing — while Luke and John present the tomb event as sufficient without promising a next confirming encounter.

gaps.gap: Luke alone opens the figures' speech with a rhetorical challenge-question that reframes the women's search as a category mistake ('why seek the living among the dead?', M10); Matthew and Mark open with a comfort directive; John's figures open with a grief-inquiry.
gaps.why: The opening speech-act establishes the rhetorical relationship between figure and witness and determines what the encounter is doing. Matthew and Mark open with comfort, positioning frightened witnesses as receptive recipients; Luke opens with challenge, positioning the witnesses as having made an interpretive error — seeking a living person in a place of death — that must be corrected; John opens with an inquiry into grief. For the QUD, Luke's challenge implies the resurrection was foreseeable from the category of the person being sought, a different attestation-claim than Matthew's/Mark's comfort-mode: the witnesses should have known.

gaps.gap: Luke alone has the figures include an extensive citation of the passion prediction within the speech (M13-M17), making re-activation of Jesus's prior words the centerpiece of the interpretation; Matthew and Mark cite prior speech only briefly; John's figures cite no prior speech at all.
gaps.why: Luke's figures ground the resurrection attestation not in the empty tomb alone but in the fulfillment of a remembered prophetic pattern: Son of Man must be handed over, crucified, and rise on the third day. The empty tomb is evidence only within that remembered frame. Matthew and Mark cite prior speech briefly as corroboration ('just as he said / told you') without recovering its content; John's figures cite nothing. For the QUD, Luke's speech-act transforms attestation from surprise-testimony to fulfilled-necessity — what the witnesses are asked to receive is not unprecedented news but recognition that a known prophecy has been enacted.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone has the numinous figure explicitly self-mark its message as a citable, authorially-attributed communication ('behold, I have told you,' M26), closing and owning the entire speech as a defined transmission from this source; no other account includes such a self-marking move.
gaps.why: The self-attribution converts the speech from an event of dialogue into a discourse-object with a named source: 'this message comes from this figure, and I have now delivered it.' All other accounts have the figures speak without this formal closure. For the QUD, Matthew's self-marking is what most explicitly makes the speech an act of attestation in the technical sense — a communication whose source, content, and delivery can be cited. Other accounts present speech-events; Matthew presents a citable message.

gaps.gap: No figure's speech argues the inference from the body's absence to the resurrection — all accounts present the absence-declaration and the resurrection-announcement as adjacent assertions without stating what makes the absence constitute evidence for rising rather than removal, reburial, or error.
gaps.why: The interpretive speech-act at the center of this beat performs an inference: empty tomb → he is risen. But no figure in any account states what licenses that inference — why the absence of the body evidences resurrection rather than theft, reburial, or mistaken tomb. The move from absence (MATT M15, MARK M20, LUKE M11) to resurrection-claim (MATT M16, MARK M19, LUKE M12) is assertion-without-argument in each case. John's figures do not attempt the inference at all. For the QUD, the figure's speech is the primary site of interpretation — and what all four accounts universally withhold at that site is the argument that would make the attestation logically grounded rather than merely proclaimed. The empty tomb is never explained; it is only announced.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: the sought one is identified as the crucified Jesus

gaps.gap: Matthew alone has the numinous figure assert first-person knowledge of the women's seeking before naming the crucified status ('I know that you seek Jesus,' M12), framing the identification as already known by the figure; Mark names the seeking as a declared fact without any knowledge-claim; Luke reframes the seeking as a category mistake without naming it.
gaps.why: The figure's first-person knowledge-claim establishes an epistemic asymmetry before the identification is delivered: the angel already knows who the women are looking for and that they are looking. This grounds the identification in the figure's omniscience rather than in the women's declaration or the figure's inference from the scene. For the QUD, Matthew's identification is the only one presented as known-by-the-identifier before being stated; the others withhold this epistemic framing, leaving the figure's basis for identifying the sought one unstated.

gaps.gap: Mark alone appends the geographic locator 'of Nazareth' to the name, identifying the sought one as 'Jesus of Nazareth'; Matthew uses only the proper name 'Jesus'; Luke withholds both the proper name and any geographic anchor, routing identification through the title 'Son of Man'.
gaps.why: The geographic identifier 'of Nazareth' anchors the identification in a specific historical person from a specific place, disambiguating from other bearers of the name Jesus and grounding the resurrection claim in verifiable historical geography. Matthew withholds this anchoring and relies on the name alone; Luke withholds both name and geography. For the QUD, Mark's identification is the most historically specific — the one who has been raised is the Nazarene, locatable in documented memory — and all other accounts withhold this level of historically auditable specificity.

gaps.gap: Luke alone withholds the direct identification formula ('you seek Jesus [of Nazareth] the crucified') and instead achieves the identification indirectly through a memory-activation of the passion prediction — crucifixion appearing as an element of the remembered speech (M16) rather than a declared identifier — with the identification completed by the women's own act of remembering (M18); Matthew and Mark deliver the identification as a direct declarative to the witnesses.
gaps.why: In Matthew and Mark the figure names the person directly: 'you seek Jesus the crucified.' In Luke the figures command the women to remember — crucifixion appears inside the recalled prediction (M16), and the women then recognize the connection (M18). For the QUD, Luke's identification depends on the witnesses' own cognitive act: it is validated by memory rather than delivered as external news. Matthew and Mark present the identification as authoritative testimony from the figure; Luke presents it as internal recognition activated from prior knowledge. These are different attestation structures — the former locates the authority in the numinous figure's declaration, the latter in the witnesses' corroborating memory.

gaps.gap: Luke alone identifies the sought one through the eschatological title 'Son of Man' within the cited passion prediction (M15-M17) rather than by the proper name 'Jesus'; Matthew uses only the proper name; Mark uses the proper name plus geographic locator.
gaps.why: The title 'Son of Man,' drawn from the prophetic tradition of Daniel 7, frames the identification eschatologically: the crucified one is identified as the figure whose pattern of suffering and vindication was already inscribed in scripture as necessity. The proper name 'Jesus' frames the identification personally and historically. For the QUD, Luke's identification embeds the resurrection in scriptural-prophetic necessity ('the Son of Man must be crucified and rise'), while Matthew's and Mark's identification grounds it in the name of a specific historical person. The two frames offer different answers to what is being attested: the fulfillment of a prophetic pattern (Luke) versus the fate of a named individual (Matt, Mark).

gaps.gap: No account explains why crucifixion is chosen as the primary identifying mark for the sought one rather than any other characterization — all three accounts pair the name or title with crucifixion as the essential identifier, but none states what makes this death-form the anchor of the identification.
gaps.why: Each account pairs the sought one's name or title with crucifixion as the identifying mark: 'Jesus the crucified' (Matt), 'Jesus of Nazareth the crucified' (Mark), 'Son of Man who must be crucified' (Luke). But no account explains why crucifixion — rather than healing, teaching, prophesying, or resurrection itself — is the criterion chosen to anchor the identification. The choice of crucifixion as primary identifier means the resurrection is attested specifically as an event that happened to a crucified person, and the cross-status is the pivot connecting the dead Jesus to the risen one. All three accounts present this as self-evident and withhold the logic that makes the death-form the organizing identification — which is precisely the theological claim most in need of grounding.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: his absence from the tomb is explicitly declared ('he is not here')

gaps.gap: Mark announces the resurrection before declaring the absence ('he has been raised... he is not here,' M19→M20); Matthew and Luke declare the absence before announcing the resurrection ('he is not here... for he has been raised' M15→M16; 'he is not here... he has risen' M11→M12).
gaps.why: The order determines the logical relationship between absence and resurrection. In Matthew and Luke, the sequence is 'absence → therefore risen': the empty tomb functions as evidence from which the resurrection claim follows. In Mark, the sequence is 'risen → therefore not here': the resurrection is the primary stated fact and the absence is its consequence. For the QUD, the order changes what is doing the attesting: in Matt and Luke the absence is the evidence and the resurrection is the conclusion; in Mark the resurrection is the prior given and the absence merely confirms it. These are structurally incompatible attestation chains wearing the same surface content.

gaps.gap: Matthew positions the declarer outside the tomb (the angel enthroned on the displaced stone, M5) when the absence is declared (M15); Mark and Luke position the declarer inside the burial space (young man on the right side, M13; two men standing beside the women, M6) when the equivalent declaration is made (M20; M11).
gaps.why: The declarer's position determines the epistemic mode of the absence-claim. Interior figures (Mark, Luke) speak from within the vacated space — their declaration is in principle observational, made from the location of the absence itself. Matthew's exterior angel speaks from the threshold, its authority resting on divine revelation rather than on proximity to the empty spot. For the QUD, the incompatible positions offer incompatible attestation modes for the same declaration: testimony from inside the space of absence versus testimony from a heavenly figure at the boundary. The accounts cannot all be right about where the declarer stood when the most pivotal claim was made.

gaps.gap: Matthew and Mark follow the absence declaration with an explicit directive to inspect the burial spot ('come, see the place where he lay,' M18-M20; 'look at the place where they laid him,' M21-M23), making physical verification a commanded response; Luke withholds any such verification directive after its absence declaration.
gaps.why: The verification directive converts the absence declaration from a testimonial claim into an invited act of empirical inspection: the witnesses are directed to confirm the declared absence by their own eyes at the named spot. Luke withholds this entirely — its figures declare the absence (M11) and move immediately to the resurrection announcement (M12) and the memory-command (M13). For the QUD, Matthew and Mark embed a physical check into the absence-attestation; Luke leaves the declaration standing without an offered verification, relying on the witnesses' memory of prior prophecy rather than present inspection.

gaps.gap: Luke alone precedes the absence declaration with a rhetorical challenge-question that reframes the search as a category mistake ('why do you seek the living among the dead?', M10) before the absence is named (M11); Matthew moves directly to the absence after the crucifixion-identification; Mark announces the resurrection before the absence without any prior reframing.
gaps.why: The rhetorical challenge does interpretive work before the absence is stated: it tells the witnesses that the entire frame of the search — looking in a place of death for a living person — was category-mistaken from the start. The absence is then not a surprising discovery but a predictable consequence of a conceptual error. Matthew and Mark withhold this prior reframing, presenting the absence as news to be received rather than a conclusion the women should have foreseen. For the QUD, Luke's structure implies the absence was foreseeable from the nature of the sought one; the other accounts treat it as unexpected — different claims about what kind of attestation the empty tomb provides.

gaps.gap: No account states how the declaring figure knows that 'he is not here' — the epistemic basis for the absence-declaration is withheld by all three, leaving the figure's claim to knowledge of the absence without any stated grounding.
gaps.why: The declaration 'he is not here' is the most direct evidential claim in the attestation sequence. Yet no account states how the figure knows this — whether by direct observation, prior witness, omniscient knowledge, or inference. Matthew's angel declares it from outside without having been seen to inspect the interior; Mark's young man is inside but is not said to have examined the space; Luke's two men appear beside the women inside without any prior inspection move. For the QUD, the figures speak with total authority about the absence but no account grounds that authority in an act of knowing. The most important single claim in the attestation chain is everywhere treated as self-authorizing — which is the central withholding.

gaps.gap: No account states when or how the departure from the tomb occurred — the declared absence implies a prior event (the body ceased to be here) that is universally withheld from the declaration itself and from everything surrounding it.
gaps.why: The declaration 'he is not here' is a present-tense state that implies a past event: at some moment he ceased to be here. The moment of that departure — when it happened, how it happened, whether it was witnessed — is withheld by every account carrying this beat. Matthew points forward to a Galilee reunion; Mark and Luke point backward to remembered prophecy; but none narrates or even alludes to the moment of departure from the burial space. For the QUD, every account attests the result ('not here') while universally suppressing the event ('left'). The resurrection's most physically decisive moment — the actual departure of the risen one from the tomb — is the one event no figure speaks and no witness names.

all_gaps_by_beat.beat: his resurrected/raised status is announced (typically as divine passive)

gaps.gap: All three accounts withhold the agent of the raising — no account names who raised Jesus.
gaps.why: MATT-28:M16 and M23 code the subject as 'not-stated'; MARK-16:M19 explicitly marks the divine-passive as 'the raiser deliberately withheld'; LUKE-24:M12 codes the verb as intransitive with 'the raiser unnamed.' The omission of the agent is universal and structurally enforced by three independent grammatical choices across three accounts. Directly bears on QUD: the central attestation claim — that Jesus was raised — is delivered by all three accounts in a form that suspends precisely the most theologically consequential part of the claim, namely who or what acted.

gaps.gap: Luke alone uses intransitive or formally self-rising language; Matthew and Mark use transitive divine passives that presuppose an unspoken external agent.
gaps.why: LUKE-24:M12 codes the verb as 'raise/rise' with the note that the English 'has risen' is intransitive and 'the underlying passive leaves the raiser unnamed'; LUKE-24:M17 similarly codes 'rise-again' with 'must' marking divine necessity but no named agent. MATT-28:M16, M23 and MARK-16:M19 are transitive passive constructions — something acted on Jesus. Luke's grammar formally permits a self-rising reading that Matt and Mark's grammar forecloses. Consequential for QUD: the mode of agency in the raised status is grammatically underdetermined in Luke in a way it is not in the other two carriers.

gaps.gap: Mark alone uses the perfect aspect, foregrounding the ongoing resultant state of the raised condition rather than the completed past event of raising.
gaps.why: MARK-16:M19 encodes the raised status as a present ongoing condition: 'he stands in the state of the raised.' MATT-28:M16 and M23 code a completed event ('raised-status (completed)' and 'raised-from-the-dead status') in aorist frames. LUKE-24:M12 codes 'he is alive again,' which reports current aliveness but does not dwell on the standing state. Mark alone shifts the announcement's propositional register from 'an event occurred' to 'a state now obtains,' which changes what is attested: the ongoing ontological condition of Jesus rather than the historical fact of a past action.

gaps.gap: Matthew alone doubles the resurrection announcement, delivering it twice at distinct narrative moments; Mark and Luke each state it once.
gaps.why: MATT-28:M16 delivers the raised-status announcement through the angel at the tomb; MATT-28:M23 delivers it again in the mouth of the risen Jesus himself to the women en route. Mark's announcement is confined to M19 (angelic). Luke's is confined to M12 (the two men). Matthew uniquely constructs a dual-witness structure: angelic voice plus the raised Jesus's own self-reference. This doubles the attestation weight and supplies an additional speaker-type — the raised Jesus as self-witness to his own raised status — entirely absent from Mark and Luke. Consequential for QUD: attestation is both denser and differently sourced in Matt.

gaps.gap: Luke alone grounds the resurrection announcement in a divine-necessity prior prediction ('must rise-again on the third day'), making the raised status prophetically required rather than only announced as accomplished fact.
gaps.why: LUKE-24:M17 codes 'rise-again (on the third day)' with 'must' (dei) marking divine necessity as the warrant; it is then followed by M12's accomplished-fact announcement. The necessity operator transforms the attestation: the resurrection is not only reported as having happened but as having been required to happen by prior divine logic. MATT-28:M16 and MARK-16:M19 carry no necessity frame; the announcement is bare accomplished fact. Consequential for QUD: the epistemic warrant Luke supplies for the raised status is prophetic inevitability, a category of grounding unavailable in Matt and Mark's announcements.
